lesson.title: Post Quantum Cryptography: Encrypting Against a Computer That Does Not Exist Yet
lesson.summary: Post quantum cryptography refers to cryptographic algorithms designed to stay secure even against a sufficiently powerful future quantum computer, an active area that NIST has been standardizing through a real, ongoing public process.
lesson.body:
TLS, the protocol that secures most traffic on the web, relies on cryptography basics covered earlier: public key algorithms that let two parties who have never met establish a shared secret key and verify each other's identity. The specific public key algorithms in widespread use today, RSA and elliptic curve cryptography, are considered secure because the mathematical problems they are built on, factoring very large numbers, or solving discrete logarithm problems on elliptic curves, are believed to be practically impossible for classical computers to solve in any reasonable amount of time at the key sizes actually used.

A sufficiently large, error corrected quantum computer would change that calculation. A well known result called Shor's algorithm shows that a quantum computer, if built at sufficient scale and reliability, could solve both factoring and discrete logarithm problems efficiently, which would break RSA and elliptic curve cryptography as they are used today. No quantum computer currently in existence is anywhere near capable of doing this against real world key sizes, and it is genuinely uncertain when, or even whether, one will be built at the necessary scale. But the concern is taken seriously for a specific reason: encrypted traffic captured and stored today could potentially be decrypted later, once a capable quantum computer exists, an idea often called harvest now, decrypt later. For data that needs to stay confidential for a long time, medical records, government secrets, long lived business data, that future risk matters even if it is still hypothetical today.

Post quantum cryptography is the effort to build public key algorithms based on entirely different mathematical problems, ones believed to resist attacks from both classical and quantum computers, so that systems like TLS can eventually migrate away from algorithms that a quantum computer could break. Candidate problems come from a few different families, including certain problems involving structured mathematical lattices, and constructions based purely on the properties of hash functions. NIST has been running a long, public standardization process to evaluate candidate post quantum algorithms, and it has been publishing initial standards, including a lattice based key encapsulation mechanism and more than one signature scheme. This is genuinely an active, moving area of standardization, so anyone implementing this in practice should check NIST's current published documents directly rather than relying on any single description, including this one, as the final word.

A concrete near term picture of how this reaches ordinary internet traffic is the idea of a hybrid TLS handshake: instead of switching straight from a classical key exchange algorithm to a post quantum one, a connection can use both at once, combining, say, elliptic curve Diffie Hellman with a post quantum key encapsulation mechanism, and deriving the actual session key from both results together. That way, even if one of the two algorithms turns out to have an undiscovered weakness, classical or quantum, the combined key stays safe as long as the other one holds. Several major browsers and cloud providers have already been experimenting with exactly this kind of hybrid post quantum TLS connection, treating it as a transitional step while post quantum algorithms mature and gain more real world scrutiny.
